guidance: Option 121 packs each route as a mask width, the significant destination octets and four router octets, and a client that supports it ignores the Router option — so include your default route here too. Data is capped at 255 bytes.
method: RFC 3442 encodes each route as one octet holding the subnet-mask width, then only the significant octets of the destination — width divided by eight, rounded up, so a /8 keeps one octet, a /17 keeps three and a /32 keeps all four — then four octets of router address. A width of zero carries no destination octets and is the default route; a router of 0.0.0.0 marks another subnet on the same link, which a client whose stack cannot install such a route must ignore. Destination bits below the mask are zeroed, and the page follows the client here: it writes the network address and says so when the line had host bits set. Routes are emitted in the order typed and concatenated, the data length is their total, and the full option is code 121 (0x79) plus that length octet; the Microsoft 249 (0xF9) form carries identical data. Since the length is a single octet the data cannot exceed 255 bytes, so a longer list is refused and points at RFC 3396 concatenation instead. Decoding accepts the data with or without the code and length octets, splits it at the offsets the widths dictate, and names the byte offset when a route is truncated or a width is above 32. Addresses with a leading-zero octet are refused because some tools read them as octal. No default route in the list produces a note that clients ignore the Router option when option 121 is present.
